claim: Set your hourly rate by experience tier, not by gut: roughly $20–30/hr with 1–2 years of design experience, $35–50/hr once you have a handful of successful client engagements behind you, and $60–100/hr after another year at that level.
why: New designers have no signal for what the market bears and either underprice into unsustainability or overprice out of contention; discrete tiers give a defensible anchor tied to demonstrable milestones.
when: You are quoting hourly in a high-cost market (US and economically comparable countries) and have no existing rate history to reference.
fails: The numbers are treated as universal — they are calibrated to a market where staff designers earn around $50/hr, and are far off in lower-cost markets where the equivalent figure is a fraction of that.

claim: Benchmark your rate against local designer salaries before importing any published rate ladder, and restate the tiers as a multiple of that local baseline rather than as absolute dollars.
why: Rate advice circulates globally but salaries do not; a figure that reads as fair in one market reads as absurd in another.
when: You are pricing outside the market the advice was authored in, or serving clients in a market different from your own.

claim: Advance rate tiers on evidence of completed successful engagements, not on calendar time alone — raise your rate after you can point to a set of clients you delivered for, then again after sustaining that level for roughly a year.
why: Ties price increases to accumulated proof you can show a prospect, so the raise is justifiable rather than arbitrary.
when: Deciding when it is legitimate to quote a higher number to the next prospect.

claim: Treat hourly billing as a temporary scaffold and migrate to fixed project pricing once you can estimate scope reliably; do not aim to reach the top hourly tier.
why: Hourly pays you for time spent rather than value delivered, so getting faster and better actively reduces your income — the model punishes the exact growth you are pursuing.
when: You have enough completed projects to forecast effort on comparable work with reasonable accuracy.
fails: Scope is genuinely unknowable — open-ended discovery, retainers, or first-of-kind work — where hourly correctly protects you from an unbounded fixed quote.

claim: Avoid pricing structures where your incentive and the client's incentive point in opposite directions; prefer models where both parties want the same outcome.
why: Under hourly, you profit from more hours while the client profits from fewer, so every timesheet becomes a small negotiation and erodes trust; a fixed fee makes efficiency mutually beneficial.
when: Choosing any commercial arrangement with a client, not just design fees.

claim: Default to giving the client a single hard total for the engagement rather than a rate plus an estimate.
why: Clients need to commit budget before work begins; an open-ended rate leaves them exposed to overrun and makes approval harder, while a concrete number is something they can sign off on.
when: Presenting a quote to a client who must justify the spend internally or to themselves.
fails: You cannot yet price the project accurately, in which case an honest rate beats a fixed number you will blow through.

claim: Before quoting any flat project fee, compute a break-even floor as (realistic hours to deliver) x (your hourly rate), and never quote below it.
why: A flat fee absorbs all estimation risk on your side, so you need a hard number that represents the point at which the work stops costing you money before you can negotiate anything above it.
when: Quoting a fixed price for a defined scope of design work.
fails: Scope is genuinely undefined or likely to change mid-project — a fixed floor built on a fictional hour count gives false confidence and you'll blow through it.

claim: Include meeting time and every planned revision round in the hour estimate, not just hands-on design time.
why: Calls, feedback cycles and rework are real hours that get billed to no one if you only count production; leaving them out is the most common way a profitable-looking flat fee turns into a loss.
when: Estimating duration for any client project involving collaboration or feedback.

claim: If you have no estimating history, start from published benchmark durations for common deliverables, then correct them against your own tracked hours after each project.
why: Benchmarks are a usable prior when you have no data, but they describe an average designer at an average speed, not you.
when: Early in a freelance career, or pricing a deliverable type you have not shipped before.
fails: Treating benchmarks as authoritative long after you have your own time-tracking data — your real numbers should override them.

claim: Multiply the break-even figure by a factor between 1.0 and 2.0 to get the quoted price, choosing the factor by how much non-cash value the project returns.
why: Two projects with identical scope are not identical business decisions; portfolio value, referral potential and enjoyment are real compensation, so projects that pay you in those currencies can carry a lower cash multiple.
when: Setting a flat project fee where you have discretion over the number.
fails: Applying a low multiplier to a client who merely promises exposure or future work without any evidence they can deliver it.

claim: Price a well-known client who will credibly generate referrals at or near your break-even, and price tedious or low-interest work at the top of the range.
why: The multiplier is the lever that makes desirable work accessible and undesirable work worth accepting; charging the same for both means you get more of the work you don't want.
when: Deciding between two projects of comparable scope, or setting a number for a client you actively do or don't want.
fails: Discounting for a marquee name that is not actually visible in your portfolio or does not talk to peers who could hire you.

claim: Default to the midpoint multiplier of roughly 1.5x for an ordinary client with moderate upside — e.g. a $4,000 break-even quoted at $6,000.
why: Most clients are neither career-making nor soul-crushing, so having a default anchor stops you renegotiating the whole framework on every proposal.
when: The client brings some value but nothing exceptional in either direction.

claim: Present the client a single flat number and keep the hour math and multiplier private.
why: The client's benefit from flat pricing is budget certainty; exposing the internal breakdown invites them to negotiate the inputs rather than accept the output.
when: Sending a proposal or quote for a fixed-scope project.

claim: For value-based pricing, quote a fee equal to 5–10% of the additional annual revenue your work is projected to generate, not a multiple of your hours.
why: The fee is framed as a share of the client's new profit, so both sides are paid out of value created rather than time consumed.
when: The client has an existing revenue baseline and the project plausibly moves a revenue-linked metric.
fails: There is no revenue to lift — pre-revenue startups, non-profits, or internal/brand work with no measurable commercial outcome.

claim: Before quoting value-based, do two pieces of homework with the client: estimate the size of the revenue gain, and agree what return on the fee they'd consider acceptable.
why: The fee only holds up if the client accepts your projection and sees their multiple on it; skipping this turns the number into an unanchored ask.
when: Any value-based engagement, since the price is derived from a forecast rather than an observable input.
fails: The client won't share revenue figures or engage in forecasting — then the inputs to the model don't exist.

claim: Build the quote from the client's numbers in a visible chain: baseline revenue → projected % lift → your % share → fee. Show the arithmetic rather than presenting a bare figure.
why: An explicit chain makes the fee auditable and shifts the negotiation onto the assumptions, where the client can participate, instead of onto your price.
when: Pitching value-based pricing to a client who needs to justify the spend internally.
fails: Any link in the chain is a guess you can't defend — a fabricated lift percentage makes the whole number look invented.

claim: Qualify a project for value-based pricing before quoting it: require that the outcome connects to revenue in a quantifiable way. If it doesn't, price the project as a fixed scope instead.
why: The method has a hard precondition, and forcing it onto non-commercial work produces a fee no one can justify.
when: Deciding which pricing model to use at the start of a new engagement.

claim: Keep fixed project pricing as your default fallback method, ready to use whenever hourly or value-based doesn't fit the client.
why: It has no preconditions about revenue or time tracking, so it covers the cases the other two models exclude.
when: Non-profits, pre-revenue clients, or any engagement where the commercial upside can't be estimated.

claim: When estimating any project, inflate your time estimate beyond your first instinct and resist discounting your rate — assume the work will run long and that you are undervaluing your skill.
why: Both biases run in the same direction and compound: underestimated hours combined with an underpriced rate turns a profitable project into an unprofitable one.
when: Producing any quote, under any of the three pricing models.

claim: Prefer value-based pricing as you move upmarket, because the fee tracks the client's revenue scale rather than your delivery time — the same effort earns more from a larger client.
why: Decoupling price from hours removes the ceiling that hourly billing puts on income.
when: You have a track record and are targeting clients large enough that a small percentage lift is a meaningful absolute number.
fails: Small clients, where even a generous share of a modest lift underpays the actual work — hourly or project pricing may yield more.

claim: When you have no client work, build portfolio pieces from self-initiated projects rather than waiting for real briefs — a portfolio is judged on the thinking and craft shown, not on whether the client paid.
why: Client work and self-initiated work are indistinguishable in a portfolio if the project has a real brief, constraints, and a coherent outcome; waiting for permission to start is what actually keeps beginners portfolio-less.
when: You are entering the industry, changing specialisms, or rebuilding a portfolio and have no shippable client projects.
fails: You misrepresent the work as paid client work, or you produce a piece with no defined problem behind it — a pretty artboard with no brief reads as an exercise, not a project.

claim: Start a self-initiated project from an externally generated brief (e.g. Good Brief, Sharpen) instead of inventing the subject yourself.
why: An external prompt supplies constraints you would not have chosen, which forces real design decisions and avoids defaulting to the same comfortable subject matter in every piece.
when: Beginning a portfolio piece with no client-supplied problem.
fails: You take the generated prompt literally and shallowly — the prompt is a seed, not a substitute for defining audience, goals, and scope.

claim: Choose a single niche and make every portfolio project sit inside it, rather than showing one project per industry.
why: A portfolio that addresses everyone signals expertise to no one; specialists are hired because the buyer sees their own problem already solved. Breadth reads as a lack of depth.
when: Assembling a portfolio aimed at attracting a specific kind of client or role.
fails: You are still exploring what you like, or targeting generalist in-house roles where range is the hiring signal; a niche chosen too early can be a cage.

claim: Pick a niche at the intersection of two tests: something you are genuinely interested in, and something where the clients have products worth selling and money to spend.
why: Interest sustains the unpaid work required to build the portfolio; commercial viability makes sure the niche can actually pay you back.
when: Deciding what your portfolio should specialise in.
fails: A passion niche with no budget (or a lucrative one you find dull) — either half alone predicts failure.

claim: Expand a one-line prompt into a full written brief — audience, goals, tone, deliverables, constraints — before opening the design tool; use an LLM to draft it if you have no client to interview.
why: Design decisions need something to be right against. A written brief converts an arbitrary idea into a set of criteria you can defend in a case study.
when: Any self-initiated project where no stakeholder exists to supply requirements.
fails: You accept generic LLM output uncritically — an unedited, hedge-filled brief produces bland design and gives the case study nothing specific to point at.

claim: Gather visual reference deliberately after the brief is written, not before, pulling from multiple platforms (Dribbble, Behance, Pinterest, Instagram) rather than one.
why: Reference collected after the brief gets filtered by the brief's constraints instead of dictating them; sampling several sources avoids inheriting one platform's house style.
when: Kicking off the visual phase of a project.
fails: Reference substitutes for a concept — copying a trending aesthetic that contradicts the brief's audience or tone.

claim: Sequence portfolio projects as niche → brief → reference → design; do not start in the design tool.
why: Each step narrows the decision space for the next, so by the time you design, most open questions are already closed and the work has a rationale attached.
when: Producing any speculative portfolio piece.
fails: Highly exploratory or style-development work, where making first and rationalising later is the point.

claim: Fill every text field in a fabricated project with plausible, domain-specific copy — real product names, real-sounding prices, real microcopy — and never ship placeholder Latin.
why: A viewer judges a self-initiated project on whether it reads as a real product; placeholder text signals the work stopped at the visual layer and no one thought about content, which also hides whether the layout survives real string lengths.
when: Any portfolio piece built from an invented brief rather than a paying client.

claim: Pick the hosting platform from the artefact type: shot-style interface work goes on Dribbble, long-form case studies go on Behance, and anything needing narrative plus personality goes on a Notion site or a custom personal site.
why: Each platform's default layout and audience expectation favours a different depth of content — a gallery grid flattens a case study, and a long-scroll format wastes a single strong screen.
when: Deciding where to publish finished work with no existing web presence.

claim: Treat a custom personal site as the target and a Notion-based site as the acceptable substitute; choose the substitute whenever build time would otherwise delay publishing.
why: A bespoke site reads as most professional but consumes time that produces no new portfolio work; shipping visible work sooner beats an unpublished perfect container.
when: Early-career designers with no clients, weighing site-building effort against making more work.
fails: Once you have enough work and time that a custom site itself becomes a demonstration of your craft — then the effort pays for itself.

claim: Cap the portfolio at two to three full case studies, or three to four pieces if you are only showing final interfaces.
why: Reviewers skim; a small set forces every piece to earn its place, and depth of reasoning in a few projects is more persuasive than breadth of thumbnails. Case studies each demand more reading time, so fewer are needed.
when: Assembling a first portfolio for job or freelance applications.

claim: Cut any project that is not among your strongest — the portfolio is judged on its weakest visible piece, not its average.
why: Every additional piece invites comparison; a mediocre entry sets the reviewer's estimate of your ceiling downward.
when: Choosing which of several finished projects to publish.

claim: Publish self-initiated work without disclaiming that it is unpaid or invented; present it with the same framing as commissioned work.
why: The evaluation is of design decisions and craft, which are identical whether or not money changed hands; flagging it as practice invites it to be discounted.
when: You have no client work yet and need something to show.
fails: Actively claiming a real client relationship or shipped status that does not exist — that is a misrepresentation, not framing.

claim: Before designing, identify the client's business problem behind the request — ask what outcome (more leads, more customers, higher order value) the site must produce, and treat 'we need a website' as a symptom, not the brief.
why: Clients pay for the result the site produces, not the artifact; a brief taken at face value produces a deliverable nobody can value.
when: Discovery, scoping, and pitching client work — especially for small business owners who describe the deliverable rather than the goal.
fails: Projects where the outcome genuinely is the artifact — internal tools, editorial or portfolio sites, spec work, or a rebuild with a fixed brand mandate — where inventing a conversion goal distorts the job.

claim: Price and pitch work against the revenue it is expected to generate, not against hours spent or number of pages delivered.
why: If the buyer sees a small spend returning a larger return, the fee stops being a cost and becomes an investment, which raises the ceiling on what they'll pay.
when: Proposals for revenue-driven businesses where you can point to a plausible mechanism for how the site increases sales.
fails: When you can't credibly attribute revenue to the site, or the client's success depends mostly on factors outside the design (traffic, product, sales team) — overpromising here sets up a failed engagement.

claim: Treat visual quality as a necessary gate, not a sufficient one: a page must pass a credibility check on looks AND move the visitor toward a specific action, and a design that satisfies only one of those is unfinished.
why: Poor visuals cost trust before the content is read, but a beautiful page with no job to do gives the visitor nothing to convert on — both failure modes end in no sale.
when: Evaluating or critiquing any commercial page — landing pages, marketing sites, product pages.
fails: Not addressed in this segment.

claim: Reject the aesthetics-versus-conversion trade-off as a false choice; when a decision seems to force it, look for the option that serves both rather than picking a side.
why: The two are framed as competing budgets, but exemplars like Apple demonstrate a single page can be both visually strong and commercially effective.
when: Design decisions where 'this looks better but converts worse' is being used to justify dropping one goal.
fails: Genuine hard constraints — performance budgets, accessibility floors, or platform limits — where something must actually give, and the visual is the correct thing to cut.

claim: Use a widely known commercial site as a reference standard when arguing a design position, so the critique rests on a shared, observable example rather than personal taste.
why: A recognisable exemplar makes the beauty-plus-purpose claim demonstrable instead of assertable.
when: Justifying design decisions to clients or in teaching contexts where taste arguments stall.
fails: When the reference brand's context differs sharply from the client's — Apple's constraints, budget, and existing demand don't transfer to a small local business.

claim: When client aesthetic preferences and end-user task completion conflict, resolve in favour of task completion — treat the client as the buyer and the end user as the person whose success the design is accountable to.
why: The people who determine whether the site produces business results are the users, not the person approving the mockup; a beautiful site that obstructs the user's task fails commercially even if the client is happy.
when: Client work where the deliverable is a functioning product (e-commerce, tools, service sites) and the client is not a representative user.
fails: Brand-expression work — fashion, luxury, portfolio, campaign microsites — where perceived aesthetic status is the actual function; also fails as an excuse for neglecting craft, since the goal is to serve the user, not to lower the visual bar.

claim: Judge an interface first on whether the primary task completes correctly and quickly; only after that is verified, spend effort on visual refinement.
why: Users tolerate significant visual and even intrusive-advertising friction when the core job is done reliably and fast, which means speed and correctness carry more weight than polish in retention.
when: Utility-driven products where users arrive with one specific job to do: converters, search, calculators, booking, checkout.
fails: Discovery-driven or trust-sensitive contexts where visual credibility is itself a precondition for the user attempting the task at all.

claim: Frame design decisions as marketing arguments — what outcome does this produce for the business and its customers — rather than as creative preferences.
why: Framing in outcome terms gives you a shared standard with the client that isn't taste, so disagreements resolve on evidence about users rather than on who has better instincts.
when: Presenting or defending design work to a client, and when deciding between two options that both look acceptable.
fails: Explicit brand-identity or art-direction engagements where the client has hired you for a creative point of view.

claim: Write your positioning as a single sentence in the form 'I help [specific industry segment] [achieve a specific outcome]' instead of describing yourself as a general-purpose designer.
why: A narrow, named segment lets a prospect recognise themselves immediately and signals that you already understand their category's recurring problems.
when: Building a designer's own site, profile, or outreach message when trying to attract a particular type of client.
fails: Early on when you have no delivered work in any segment, or when the chosen niche is too small to sustain a pipeline.

claim: Derive your niche from the operational problems that a real past or current client faced, not from an industry label you find appealing.
why: Concrete constraints — for example a retailer with hundreds of products, where navigation, filtering and findability dominate — give you specific problems to speak to, which is what makes a pitch credible.
when: Choosing a specialisation after you have at least one project in a given industry.
fails: When the single client's situation is atypical for the industry and generalising from it misleads you.

claim: For catalogue sites with large product counts, treat findability — search, filtering, category structure — as the primary design problem rather than the homepage's visual impression.
why: The scale of the inventory means a user's success depends almost entirely on being able to reach the right item, so that is where the design effort produces revenue.
when: E-commerce or directory sites with product counts in the hundreds or more.
fails: Small curated catalogues where the whole range fits on one or two screens and browsing beats filtering.

claim: Structure every portfolio case study in three fixed sections: the services you delivered, the specific problem the client had, and the solution with its measured outcome.
why: A fixed skeleton forces the narrative onto business impact rather than visual showcase, and gives prospects a repeatable way to map their own situation onto your past work.
when: Writing portfolio entries, proposals, or pitch decks for freelance and studio client acquisition.
fails: Projects where you were handed a spec with no diagnosed problem, or NDA work where outcomes cannot be disclosed — the skeleton then has an empty middle or end.

claim: Attach at least one number to the outcome of each case study — conversion rate, bounce rate, revenue, session length — rather than describing the result qualitatively.
why: Quantified results are hard for a prospect to dispute or discount, whereas adjectives about a redesign read as self-assessment.
when: Any client work where before/after measurement was possible.
fails: When the number is unflattering, cherry-picked from a short window, or confounded by a simultaneous marketing push — a weak number invites scrutiny that a qualitative framing avoids.

claim: Default to framing the client's problem as a specific leak in the path to conversion (e.g. drop-off at checkout, unclear entry point) rather than as a general aesthetic deficiency.
why: A conversion-shaped problem statement makes the redesign measurable and ties it to money the client already understands.
when: Commercial sites — e-commerce, lead-gen, booking — where a funnel exists.
fails: Brand, editorial, or internal-tool projects where the goal is perception or task efficiency, not conversion; forcing a funnel frame there misdescribes the work.

claim: Before starting a client project, secure a route to the site's analytics — either by building the site yourself or by negotiating dashboard access as part of the engagement.
why: Without measurement access you cannot produce the numeric proof that the next pitch depends on, so each project fails to compound into sales material.
when: Freelance or small-studio design engagements intended to build a portfolio.
fails: Large projects with a dedicated engineering team, where analytics ownership sits elsewhere and access must be requested rather than assumed.

claim: Extend your offering from design-only to design-plus-build, using either hand-written code or a website builder, so you deliver the live site rather than a handoff file.
why: Clients on small projects don't want to broker communication between a designer and a separate developer, and shipping the site yourself keeps you attached to the outcome data.
when: Small-to-mid client projects — marketing sites, boutique e-commerce, portfolios.
fails: Complex builds with custom backends, integrations, or compliance needs, where specialist engineering is genuinely warranted and a solo design-build attempt degrades quality.

claim: Treat a site builder's basic built-in analytics as sufficient for case-study evidence instead of blocking on a full analytics stack.
why: The pitch needs a credible directional number, not statistical rigour, so the default reporting most builders ship already clears the bar.
when: Small client sites where no analytics tooling exists yet.
fails: Claims that require attribution, cohorting, or segmentation, which basic builder dashboards cannot support.

claim: Keep the case study to a short outline — a few lines per section — rather than a long-form write-up.
why: Prospects skim; the artifact's job is to demonstrate you diagnose and measure, which a brief outline conveys as well as an essay.
when: Portfolio pages and first-contact sales material.
fails: Deeper credibility contexts — agency RFPs or awards submissions — that expect process detail.

claim: Sell design and development as a single end-to-end engagement rather than design-only deliverables handed to someone else's developer.
why: Clients are buying relief from coordination overhead, not just artefacts; one point of contact removes the handoff, the translation losses, and the management time they don't have.
when: Pitching small-business or owner-operated clients who have no in-house technical team and no project manager
fails: The client already employs a dev team or has an established build pipeline, where inserting yourself into implementation creates friction rather than removing it

claim: Negotiate continuing analytics access as part of the engagement — request admin or, if that's resisted, view-only permissions on the site's analytics property before the project ends.
why: Without persistent access you lose the only instrument that can tell you whether your design worked; asking after launch is much harder than folding it into the original scope.
when: Any engagement where you build or deploy the site and want evidence of results
fails: Clients with data-handling or privacy constraints who cannot grant third-party access to visitor data

claim: Capture a baseline of the client's key metrics before you change anything, then compare the same metrics over a comparable window after launch.
why: A redesign's value is only demonstrable as a delta; without a pre-change measurement, any post-launch number is unattributable and your claim of impact is just assertion.
when: Redesigns and refreshes of existing sites that already have live traffic
fails: Brand-new sites with no traffic history, or when seasonality, ad spend changes, or PR spikes confound the comparison window

claim: Anchor your design goals to two business outcomes — time visitors spend on the site, and conversions such as sales or signups — and let those drive design decisions.
why: Businesses buy websites to make money, so the metrics you optimise are the vocabulary that connects your craft decisions to their purchasing decision.
when: Scoping, pitching, or justifying design work to a commercial client
fails: Goals that legitimately conflict with dwell time, e.g. support or documentation pages where faster task completion is better than longer sessions

claim: Offer the client an ongoing service tied to the site so your continued access has a stated reason.
why: Access is granted in exchange for value; a maintenance, monitoring, or iteration retainer makes staying on the account normal rather than an unexplained lingering permission.
when: After launch, when you want to keep measuring and keep the relationship open for further work

claim: Treat pre-launch UX testing as directional input, not as proof of impact, unless you can recruit a genuinely large participant pool.
why: Small samples produce results that don't generalise, so they can't substantiate a claim about business outcomes the way live traffic data can.
when: Deciding what evidence to present to a client to justify design choices
fails: Qualitative usability testing, where a handful of participants is the correct method for surfacing blocking problems and no statistical claim is being made

claim: Build measurement into the project plan itself: agree the metrics, secure access, record the baseline, ship, then report the comparison.
why: Retrofitting evidence after the fact is usually impossible; the sequence only works if the instrumentation step precedes the design work.
when: Structuring a client engagement from proposal through post-launch reporting

claim: Do not treat visual polish and functional problem-solving as a tradeoff to be budgeted against each other; ship both, because perceived usability rises with perceived beauty.
why: The aesthetic-usability effect: users judge attractive interfaces as easier to use, which buys tolerance for minor friction and increases time spent on the page.
when: Deciding where to spend effort on a client site or portfolio piece, especially when tempted to justify a plain design as 'function over form'.
fails: Aesthetics are used as a substitute for fixing real usability defects — the halo masks small problems from users but does not remove them, and it can hide broken flows from the designer during testing.

claim: When citing a design principle to a client or in your own reasoning, name the documented effect and let the other party verify it rather than asserting taste.
why: A named, researched phenomenon converts a subjective preference into a defensible argument, which is what makes visual work billable.
when: Justifying design decisions to non-designer stakeholders who see visual work as decoration.

claim: Treat 'time on site' as a legitimate outcome of visual quality and track it as a business metric alongside conversion.
why: The narration frames attractiveness as a retention tool, meaning visual investment has a measurable analytics signature rather than only an emotional one.
when: Reporting design work back to a client who needs a business rationale.
fails: Time on site is a poor metric for task-completion interfaces, where lower dwell time signals success.

claim: Only include portfolio pieces you would voluntarily show to friends and family; cut anything you'd need to explain away or apologize for.
why: A crowded field means work is filtered by its weakest visible item, and pride is a usable proxy for whether a piece clears the bar.
when: Curating a portfolio for job applications in a competitive entry-level market.
fails: Applied so strictly that a beginner ships nothing — early on you still need volume to have anything to curate from, and personal embarrassment can undervalue work that reads fine to outsiders.

claim: Before applying, read your own resume and portfolio in one pass as if you were the hiring manager for the role, and answer yes or no to 'would I hire this person'; treat every hesitation as a named gap to fix.
why: Self-assessment from the maker's seat rewards effort and intent; assessment from the hirer's seat only rewards evidence, which is what actually gets evaluated.
when: Preparing application materials, especially when applications aren't converting to interviews.
fails: Used as an open-ended confidence check rather than producing a concrete list of fixes — it becomes discouragement instead of a work plan.

claim: Research what a specific company is hiring for and reframe your existing work against those criteria, rather than presenting the portfolio as a neutral highlight reel.
why: Companies and independent designers weigh work differently, so unframed work gets judged against criteria you never addressed.
when: Moving from self-directed or freelance practice into applications for in-house or agency roles.
fails: Reframing slides into misrepresentation, or the portfolio is rewritten so narrowly for one employer that it stops working for any other.

claim: Present self-taught work with the structure a corporate reviewer expects — stated problem, constraints, process, and outcome — instead of showing finished visuals alone.
why: Skills picked up in an unstructured way are real but illegible to a structured hiring process unless they're packaged in that process's vocabulary.
when: Transitioning from independent or self-directed learning into a structured corporate environment.
fails: The added structure becomes filler case-study boilerplate around work that has no real reasoning behind it.

claim: Put a photo of yourself in the first viewport of a portfolio site, not buried on an About page.
why: A portfolio sells a person, not just artifacts; a face establishes who the visitor is dealing with before they evaluate the work, and it is the pattern shared across professional portfolios.
when: Personal/freelance portfolio sites where the visitor is a recruiter or client deciding whether to trust an individual.
fails: Not addressed in this segment.

claim: Treat a short looping video of yourself as an upgrade over a still headshot, but only if you are comfortable on camera — otherwise ship the still.
why: Motion draws attention and reads as more personal, but an awkward on-camera presence undercuts the credibility the photo exists to build, so the still is the safer default.
when: Hero sections where you already have or can produce comfortable on-camera footage.
fails: When you are self-conscious on camera; a forced video is worse than a good still.

claim: Shoot your own headshot rather than skipping it: pick a plain, non-competing backdrop — a blank wall, a bookshelf, or your desk setup — before worrying about gear.
why: The barrier to having a headshot is perceived difficulty, not equipment; location choice does most of the work by keeping the background from competing with the face.
when: You have no professional headshot and no budget for a photographer.
fails: Not addressed in this segment.

claim: Limit the hero intro to two facts — your name and what you do — and cut everything else out of the first screen.
why: Visitors decide within seconds whether you are relevant to them; anything beyond identity and role delays that judgement and gets skipped anyway.
when: The above-the-fold intro block on a portfolio or personal site.
fails: Not addressed in this segment.

claim: Build a portfolio hero by copying conventions observed across several professional portfolios rather than inventing a novel layout.
why: Recurring patterns across pro sites are evidence of what works for this audience; the differentiation should come from the work shown, not from an unfamiliar structure.
when: Designing a portfolio when you lack a reliable read on what recruiters or clients expect.
fails: Not addressed in this segment.

claim: In a portfolio hero, state your name and what you do in plain language, and remove every element that does not serve that statement.
why: A first-time visitor's only job at the top of the page is to learn who you are and whether you do the thing they need; ornament competes with that answer and delays it.
when: Designing the above-the-fold section of a personal or freelance portfolio site.
fails: Sites where identity is already established (a returning-client dashboard, a brand's own site) or where the hero's job is to sell a product rather than a person.

claim: Limit a portfolio to two or three top-level pages — home, contact, and optionally about — rather than splitting content across many routes.
why: A portfolio's job is a single linear pitch; extra pages fragment that pitch and add navigation decisions the visitor gains nothing from making.
when: Structuring the information architecture of an individual's portfolio site.
fails: Portfolios with many deep case studies, where each project reasonably earns its own page, or sites that double as a blog or shop.

claim: Make every page and layout's purpose predictable from its label and position; if a visitor cannot guess what a page contains before clicking, cut it or fold it into an existing page.
why: Confusion in navigation reads as carelessness in the work itself, which is the opposite of what a portfolio is arguing.
when: Deciding whether a proposed section deserves to be its own route.

claim: Treat portfolio conventions as a set to satisfy in majority, not in full — deliberately breaking one convention is fine when the rest of the page still does its job.
why: The rules are heuristics derived from what usually works, not requirements; the owner's judgement about their own presentation outranks any single item on the list.
when: Evaluating a portfolio against a checklist of best practices, or deciding whether to adopt a convention that fights your own content.
fails: When breaking a convention is a rationalisation for skipping work rather than a considered choice — a portfolio that violates most conventions is not exercising judgement.

claim: Fold about-page content into the homepage by default, and only promote it to its own page when it has grown past what the homepage can carry.
why: The narrator's own two-page site is offered as sufficient, with about framed as a permitted addition rather than a baseline component.
when: Deciding where biography and background material lives on a small personal site.

claim: If your body of work is small (roughly a handful of projects), build the portfolio as a single scrolling page with anchor navigation instead of separate routed pages.
why: Splitting thin content across multiple pages makes each page feel empty and adds navigation cost for no informational gain; one page keeps the whole story continuous.
when: Early-career or focused portfolios with limited case-study material, or when simplicity is an explicit goal.
fails: Deep case studies, many projects, or content that needs its own URL for sharing and SEO — those outgrow a single page and become an endless scroll.

claim: In a single-page portfolio, make header links jump to in-page sections rather than navigating away, so the visitor never leaves the page.
why: Preserving one continuous surface keeps orientation intact and removes page-load interruptions between sections.
when: Any single-page layout with more than one distinct section (work, about, contact).
fails: Sections long enough that anchor jumps disorient the user without a persistent nav or scroll indicator.

claim: Lead each project entry with a large image — full-width or full-bleed — sized to dominate the viewport rather than sitting as a thumbnail beside text.
why: Visitors scan a portfolio visually before reading any copy, so the image is the element that actually earns their attention and stops the scroll.
when: Portfolio index pages and project headers where the work is visual (UI, branding, product, photography).
fails: Work whose value is not visible in a screenshot — research, systems, writing — where an oversized image oversells a weak visual and the reasoning must lead instead.

claim: Set an explicit visual hierarchy where imagery is primary and project text is secondary: keep captions and descriptions short, smaller, and lower-contrast than the image they support.
why: If copy competes with the image for attention, neither wins; subordinating text lets the eye land on the work first and read only after it's interested.
when: Project listings and case-study intros where the image is the selling point.
fails: Detail sections deeper in a case study, where process and reasoning are the actual content and text should take the lead.

claim: Use saturated, high-impact colour in hero imagery to increase stopping power on scroll.
why: Bright colour raises the visual salience of an image so it registers during fast scanning.
when: Above-the-fold or first-project imagery where you need to capture attention immediately.
fails: Portfolios with a deliberately restrained or monochrome brand, where loud colour reads as inconsistent with the work itself.

claim: Break a case study into short prose blocks and place a supporting visual (still, GIF, or screen recording) after every one to two paragraphs, rather than grouping images into a gallery or leaving long unbroken text.
why: Visitors skim; interleaved imagery keeps the narrative legible at scroll speed and lets each visual carry the point the adjacent text is making instead of forcing the reader to reconstruct the link.
when: Writing a process case study for a portfolio in a visual discipline — product design, UI, branding, illustration, motion.
fails: Filler screenshots with no informational content dilute the cadence; the rule is about a visual per idea, not a fixed image quota. Non-visual disciplines (research, writing, strategy) may legitimately lean on text plus diagrams.

claim: Validate a case study by scrolling it with the text ignored: if the images alone do not convey the problem, the process, and the outcome, the visuals are under-doing their job and need to be added to or replaced.
why: Most visitors never read the copy, so the image sequence is the version of the story that actually gets consumed; it has to stand on its own.
when: Reviewing or critiquing any portfolio case study before publishing.

claim: Make the portfolio's dominant medium match the medium of the work being sold — if the output is visual, lead with artifacts (screens, prototypes, motion) and treat writing as caption and connective tissue.
why: The portfolio is itself a sample of the work; describing visual output in words asks the viewer to take the craft on faith instead of showing evidence of it.
when: Deciding the content mix and page structure of a personal portfolio or project page.
fails: Reasoning-heavy roles still need the decision trail written out; stripping text entirely turns a case study into a gallery and hides the thinking hiring managers are checking for.

claim: End each case study with a short reflection section covering what was learned or what would be done differently.
why: It signals self-awareness and growth beyond the polished result, and gives the reader a closing takeaway instead of an abrupt stop at the final mockup.
when: Structuring the tail end of a project write-up, especially for junior or career-change portfolios where learning trajectory matters.

claim: Use animated GIFs or short loops for anything with state, transition, or interaction; reserve stills for static artefacts.
why: A static frame cannot show a flow or a motion decision, so the viewer has to imagine it — the exact gap the visual is meant to close.
when: Documenting prototypes, micro-interactions, flows, or before/after transitions in a case study.
fails: Heavy or autoplaying loops throughout a long page hurt load time and readability; use them selectively where motion is the point.

claim: End each case study with a short 'what I'd do differently' section naming a specific decision you would revisit and why.
why: Admitting a revisable decision signals self-awareness and an ongoing learning practice, which reads as competence rather than weakness to someone deciding whether to hire you.
when: Any project write-up where the process is on display and the outcome is not flawless.
fails: Vague self-flagellation with no specific alternative, or a critique so severe it makes the shipped work look unusable, undercuts rather than builds trust.

claim: Include case studies only if your discipline sells the reasoning path; if it sells the artefact, lead with the artefact instead.
why: Case studies exist to make invisible decision-making legible. Where the final piece already demonstrates the skill being bought, narrating process adds reading cost without adding evidence.
when: Deciding portfolio format at the outset — UX and product design justify full case studies; graphic design, UI-only work, and copywriting often do not.
fails: A visual discipline where the client is specifically buying strategy or systems thinking (brand systems, design ops) — there the process does need showing.

claim: Pick portfolio structure from what your buyer needs to evaluate, not from the format your peers use.
why: Portfolio conventions are inherited rather than reasoned; copying a UX case-study template into a visual portfolio imports work that does not serve the reader.
when: Structuring or restructuring a personal portfolio site.
fails: Applying for roles at organisations with a stated portfolio format requirement, where the convention is a filter you must pass.

claim: Write the about page in first person and plain speech, aimed at building a human connection rather than restating your CV.
why: The about page is where a prospect decides whether they want to work with you, a judgement made on personality and fit that the project pages cannot carry.
when: Portfolios whose goal is client acquisition or freelance enquiries.

claim: Treat the about page as optional and skip it if you cannot write something genuinely personal.
why: A generic about page occupies prime navigation space while communicating nothing a visitor could not infer from the work.
when: Portfolios where the work itself is the whole pitch.

claim: Add a dated, running personal update section to your portfolio alongside the work — a short log of what's actually happening in your life, not a changelog of projects.
why: Case-study sections converge on the same competent, interchangeable voice; a life update is unique to you and is what a visitor recalls after closing twenty tabs.
when: Personal portfolio or about page for an individual designer, developer, or freelancer competing against many similar-looking sites.
fails: Team, agency, or client-facing corporate sites where the reader is buying an organisation, not a person; also fails if the log goes stale, since an update dated eighteen months ago signals abandonment.

claim: In personal updates, include the unflattering and mundane events — being laid off, getting sick, an aimless trip — not just wins and launches.
why: Setbacks are what make the writing read as honest rather than as marketing; a log of only wins reads as another highlight reel and earns no trust.
when: Writing the personal/now/update section of a portfolio, once you've decided to include one.
fails: When the disclosure would damage you professionally or expose other people — candour is the goal, oversharing and airing grievances about named clients or employers is not.

claim: Pair the personal writing with a real photo of yourself; treat face and story as one trust device rather than two separate features.
why: A face makes the writing attributable to a person and the writing gives the face a history — either alone is weaker than the pair.
when: Any solo portfolio where the goal is being hired or remembered by a human reader.

claim: Write a one-line self-description built from three or four concrete, specific enthusiasms rather than abstract professional values.
why: Named objects — a furniture brand, houseplants, a particular design principle — are things a reader can picture and react to; 'passionate about clean design' gives them nothing to hold.
when: Hero line, footer, or about blurb on a personal portfolio.
fails: When the list is generic enough to belong to anyone in the field, at which point it adds words without adding a person.

claim: Choose personality details that some readers will disagree with, and don't sand them down for universal appeal.
why: The point is giving the reader something to have a reaction to; a detail everyone accepts produces no reaction and is therefore forgettable. Divisive-but-harmless taste is the target, not consensus.
when: Deciding how much of your actual taste to expose in portfolio copy.
fails: Where the divisive material is political or identity-based rather than a matter of taste — that trades memorability for lost opportunities, which is not the bargain being described.

claim: Assume visitors will scroll past the work section, so place the human material where it can still be found — a dedicated section further down the page rather than buried on a secondary about page.
why: In the example, the memorable content sits below the work and still lands; what matters is that it exists on the main scroll, not that it leads.
when: Single-page or scroll-driven portfolio layouts.
fails: Long portfolios where anything below three or four screens will not be reached without a nav anchor.

claim: When a portfolio is stale, say so plainly on the page (e.g. a one-line note that it hasn't been updated since a given year) instead of hiding it or apologising in a disclaimer buried in the footer.
why: A visitor will notice dated work anyway; naming it first turns a perceived weakness into a signal of self-awareness and honesty, which is a trait people hire for. Concealment reads as either oblivious or evasive.
when: Your portfolio's newest case study is significantly older than the work you'd be hired to do, and you can't refresh it before it goes in front of people.
fails: The candour becomes the whole message — if the note is the most memorable thing on the site and the work itself shows nothing, honesty just efficiently communicates that there's nothing to see. It also fails in contexts where the reader has no tolerance for it, such as an application screened against a rubric.

claim: Design personality moments to be *quotable* — the test is whether a visitor could describe the detail to someone else a week later.
why: The stated objective is that people remember the portfolio and return to it. A generic 'about me' paragraph is not retellable; a specific, slightly risky admission is.
when: Adding voice, humour, or personal disclosure to any personal site or portfolio.
fails: Memorability is pursued for its own sake with gimmicks unconnected to the work or the person, which produces recall of the trick rather than the maker.

claim: Build a personal reference library by scrolling through portfolios you admire *before* you start designing yours, rather than designing from a blank page and searching for inspiration when you get stuck.
why: Studying a set of executed examples gives you concrete patterns and a quality bar to aim at; starting cold means reinventing solved problems and anchoring on whatever template you happen to open.
when: Beginning work on a portfolio or any personal-brand site.

claim: Design every case-study section to make both the problem-to-solution reasoning and your prospective value to an employer evident.
why: A case study functions both as evidence of how you solve problems and as a hiring signal.
when: Creating a portfolio case study for graphic design, product design, UX design, or UX research work.

claim: Write the problem statement as a concise description of a specific user group, their context, and the need or outcome they are trying to achieve.
why: A precise problem keeps the project focused on a real need and makes the proposed solution meaningful.
when: Opening a UX case study or framing a design project before presenting the process.
fails: It is based on an unvalidated assumption or is so broad that it cannot guide design decisions.

claim: Validate the problem before developing or presenting a solution.
why: A well-executed solution has little value if it addresses the wrong problem or no real problem at all.
when: Defining project scope, choosing which user need to prioritize, and preparing a case-study narrative.

claim: Place a short, plain-language solution summary immediately after the problem near the top of the case study.
why: Hiring managers and clients can understand the outcome without needing to read the entire process first.
when: Creating a portfolio case study intended for fast review by employers or clients.
fails: The summary exposes confidential work or makes an exploratory project appear more final than it is.

claim: Support the problem statement with synthesized research findings rather than presenting it as an unsupported assertion.
why: Grouping evidence into recurring themes makes the rationale for the problem credible and traceable.
when: You have qualitative responses, interviews, surveys, or other user data to interpret.
fails: The source data is too limited, biased, or unrelated to the target users.

claim: Use an affinity map or similar clustering exercise to turn raw research into common themes, then derive the problem statement from those themes.
why: Pattern grouping connects individual observations to a defensible problem definition.
when: Synthesizing qualitative research for a UX project.
fails: Themes are imposed before reviewing the evidence or are not represented by the collected data.

claim: Start lightweight research with a simple questionnaire when formal research is not practical, then use the responses as input to synthesis.
why: Collecting initial user input need not require a complex research operation.
when: Early-stage or small-scope projects with limited time and resources.
fails: Friends and family are not representative of the intended users and their responses are treated as conclusive validation.

claim: Treat the visual presentation of a case study as a core deliverable; make it polished enough to invite reading.
why: Viewers may dismiss or skip valuable content when its presentation looks careless.
when: Creating portfolio case studies or other documents meant to communicate design work to reviewers.

claim: Break up text-heavy case-study sections with concise copy and supporting images or animated demonstrations that clarify the work.
why: Visual evidence makes the narrative faster to scan and easier to understand than text alone.
when: Explaining flows, iterations, interfaces, or outcomes in a UX case study.
fails: When visuals are decorative, redundant, or distract from the argument.

claim: Make every chart self-explanatory by adding a title, labelled axes, and a legend where multiple series or encodings require one.
why: Readers cannot correctly interpret data without knowing what the chart and its visual encodings represent.
when: Presenting research, metrics, survey results, or product outcomes visually.
fails: A legend is unnecessary when there is only one unambiguous data series.

claim: Use annotations such as circles or callouts to direct attention to the data point that supports your case-study argument.
why: Guided attention reduces the effort required to identify the relevant finding.
when: A graph contains a specific trend, comparison, or outlier that the reader should notice.
fails: When annotations obscure data or imply more certainty than the evidence supports.

claim: For each final design view, place nearby copy that explains the design decision and the problem it solves.
why: Finished visuals alone may not communicate the rationale or demonstrate why the solution is effective.
when: Presenting final screens, flows, or prototypes in a UX case study.

claim: Display final UI images as large as the available layout reasonably allows, preserving enough detail for inspection.
why: Viewers need to read interface details in order to understand and assess the underlying design decisions.
when: Showing screens or detailed interface states in a portfolio case study.
fails: A large image would conceal necessary comparison context or make the case study difficult to navigate.

claim: Use progressive-disclosure controls such as clickable tabs to organize supporting rationale without overwhelming the main visual presentation.
why: They can let viewers access explanations for important choices while keeping the design showcase focused.
when: A design has several decisions or variants that need explanation alongside the final outcome.

claim: Include a dedicated reflection section that names concrete limitations, decisions you would change, and improvements for a future iteration.
why: It demonstrates critical self-assessment and makes the project narrative more credible.
when: Documenting a completed UX or product-design project in a portfolio case study.
fails: Do not use it as a vague apology or an unprioritized list of every possible flaw.

claim: Briefly describe meaningful project difficulties and what you learned from them.
why: Showing how you responded to constraints helps readers understand your judgment, not just the polished outcome.
when: The work involved notable trade-offs, uncertainty, or execution challenges.
fails: Avoid including routine friction that does not affect the design, process, or future approach.

claim: Call out weak or non-representative research sampling and state how you would improve it next time.
why: Early research often relies on convenient participants such as friends and family, which can limit validity.
when: Research participants are small, convenient, homogeneous, or otherwise not representative of intended users.
fails: Do not frame a biased sample as sufficient evidence for broad user claims.

claim: List important features or content deferred because of time or scope as prioritized future work.
why: This distinguishes deliberate scoping from omissions and creates a clear path for iteration.
when: Useful work was intentionally left out of the first version.
fails: Avoid presenting unvalidated feature ideas as guaranteed next steps.

claim: Keep the reflection and conclusion short, selecting only the most consequential insights.
why: A concise, high-signal close is more effective than a lengthy recap.
when: Closing any portfolio case study.
fails: Brevity fails if it removes the evidence needed to understand the main limitation or learning.

claim: Describe meaningful setbacks, discoveries, and decision points in the order they occurred so the case study has a narrative arc.
why: A genuine story adds personality and holds attention better than a flat process report.
when: The project included real uncertainty, iterations, testing moments, or a clear insight that changed the direction.
fails: Do not manufacture drama or include incidental events that do not help explain a design decision.

claim: Keep case-study copy concise and let images, video, prototypes, or other visual evidence carry information where they can.
why: A case study is consumed like a web page, where dense text discourages readers.
when: Explaining process, research, or outcomes that can be demonstrated visually.
fails: Do not omit the brief explanation needed to make visual evidence and decisions understandable.

claim: Scope the case study so a reader can finish it in one sitting, approximately 10–15 minutes.
why: A bounded reading time makes the work approachable and supports full comprehension.
when: Publishing a portfolio case study for busy reviewers or hiring teams.

claim: Use section headings that summarize the specific content or development of each section rather than generic labels.
why: Descriptive, chapter-like titles make the document easier to skim and create more interest.
when: Organizing a multi-section case study.
